Classic Judd Apatow vibes, since he produced it, but Stoller's direction is sharper. The way he shoots L A's chaos versus the Greek theater's calm, perfect metaphor.
Still can't believe this came out in what, two thousand ten? Feels timeless. You think they'd ever do a sequel? All those relapsing on a world tour.
Please, no. The ending's perfect. Aldous gets soberish, Aaron keeps his job, and we get that absurd African child music video credits. No notes.
Agreed, it's a studio comedy that shouldn't have depth, but does. Also, Rose Byrne needs more comedy roles. She stole every scene.
Hundred percent, alright. Who's rewatching this weekend? I need to catch all the background Easter eggs again.
Okay, who else stayed up thinking about Joshua last night? That movie messed me up.
Right, George Laitif doesn't get enough credit for psychological thrillers. The way he framed those family dinners to feel claustrophobic, genius.
Ugh, Sam Rockwell as Brad though. His slow unraveling from perfect dad to paranoid wreck? Masterclass. That scene where he finds the broken crib latch, chills.
But Vera Farmiga as Abby deserved an Oscar nomination. Her postpartum hallucinations, when she sees the shadow crawling toward the baby, I screamed.
Everyone's sleeping on Jacob Kogan as Joshua. That kid's creepy smile when he's holding his sister, calculated evil. How'd they make a nine year old so terrifying?
Right, I just want to help Dad, like sociopath deeds, but the ambiguity kills me. Did he poison the mom's tea or was it stress?
Nah, Latif leaves clues. Remember the kitchen drawer, Joshua's fingerprints on the meds, and the way the camera lingers on his toy soldiers? He's strategizing.
Okay, but the sister's sudden illness, the doctors said natural causes, but Joshua's science fair project was about toxins. Coincidence?
And the music, those discordant piano notes every time Joshua enters a room. Pure dread. Brad's breakdown in the rain. Sam Rockwell sobbing. Heartbreaking.
Still the ending, Joshua alone with the grandparents smiling at the new baby, chilling, makes you question nature vs nurture forever.
Think George Latif meant to critique perfect family pressure, Abby's obsession with appearances, Brad's denial?
Totally, that shot of their high rise apartment, isolated, cold. Even the wallpaper pattern looks like prison bars. Chilling.
Can we talk about the school scenes? Joshua manipulating his teacher with that concerned son act. Kid's a mini Machiavelli.
Still mad Vera Farmiga got snubbed. Her unraveling felt too real. The stained robe, unwashed hair, you believed she was drowning.
Jacob Cogan carried the third act. His monotone I love you, Mom during the hospital visit, ice cold.
Alright, who else thinks Splash is the most underrated rom com of the eighties? Tom Hanks as Allen Bauer, classic Hanks charm.
Oh totally, but Dale Hanna as Madison the mermaid, iconic. That scene where she's learning human slang in the department store, adorable and hilarious.
Ron Howard doesn't get enough credit for balancing the goofy stuff with real heart, like the underwater sequences, pure magic. Did y'all know they used practical effects for Madison's tail?
Dot, wait, but Eugene Levy as that paranoid scientist Walter Kornbluth? She's a mermaid, bauer. His delivery kills me every time. The man's a comedy genius.
Can we talk about the bittersweet stuff? When Madison has to choose between staying with Alan or returning to the ocean, Daryl Hannah nailed that sadness without saying a word. It's incredible.
Wright and John Candy as Alan's brother Freddy. His obsession with Madison's cousins in The Ocean's Peak. Candy chaos.
But the romance though, that final shot of them swimming together, I cry every time. Way deeper than fish out of water comedy.
Speaking of Ron Howard, said in an interview that the script was originally way darker. Thank God they lightened it up. Still, the theme about love versus greed in the city, low key genius.
Dot also, Madison's naivety about human stuff. Like thinking money grows on trees. Such a clever dig at eighties materialism.
Don't forget the awards. Der Ohana won that sci fi trophy, right? And the screenplay award. The dialogue's so sharp. I don't even have a pinky.
Honestly, the chemistry between Hanks and Hannah unmatched. You believe they'd risk everything for each other?
Still mad they never made a sequel. Madison adapting to the nineties, Owen learning to scuba, missed opportunity.
Nah, the ending's perfect. Open water, no guarantees, just love. Ron Howard's sweet spot.
Dot agreed. And can we appreciate how Madison's curiosity mirrors Alan's childhood wonder? Full circle storytelling.
Uh, now I need to rewatch it. Anyone up for pizza and a splash marathon tonight?
Okay, did anyone else just rewatch Hitchcock's The Man Who Knew Too Much? I forgot how intense that movie gets.
Oh totally, Alfred Hitchcock's suspense game here is unreal. James Stewart as Ben McKenna, perfect casting. That man can play desperate dad like nobody's business.

Right, but Doris Day as Jill McKenna stole it for me. The way she switches from sweet singer to mama bear mode when Hank gets kidnapped, chills. And her singing key, Sarah Sarah to signal the police, genius. That episode.
Don't sleep on the actual kidnapping scene though. When the camera lingers on the empty courtyard after Hank disappears. Pure Hitchcock. No music, just silence. Makes your stomach drop.

Y E S and the whole setup in Morocco like how casual it starts with them just vacationing meeting Louis Bernard then boom assassination plots and secret names Ambrose Chapel still sounds like a fake villain name Bernard
Classic Hitchcock misdirection. Ambrose Chapel isn't even the real threat. It's that icy woman, Brenda DeBanzie's character. Her fake politeness at the embassy dinner, so creepy.

Okay, but let's talk about the Royal Albert Hall climax. The way Hitchcock builds tension with the orchestra, the cymbals crashing, timed with the gunshot. Masterclass. Doris Day's scream echoing, haunting.
And James Stewart's face during all that, he's sweating bullets, racing to stop the assassination. You feel every second of that eight minute sequence. No C G I, no cuts, just raw suspense.
Honestly, the whole ordinary people caught in spy chaos thing, Hitchcock's trademark, but the family angle hits harder here. Like they're not agents, they're just parents trying to save their kid.
That scene where Ben breaks down yelling, what have you done to him, to the kidnapper, Stewart's delivery cracks me every time. Nineteen fifty six and it's still relatable.
Also low key genius move making Doris Day a famous singer in the plot, real life Day was a music icon, so that key Sarah Sarah moment made a perfection, won the Oscar for Best Original Song right.
Yep, but back to villains. Bernard Miles as the assassin lurking in the shadows. Underrated. His cold professionalism versus Joe's raw emotion. Perfect foil. You nailed it.
Can we talk about how Hank's actor Christopher Olson actually looks like a mini Stewart? Casting director deserves a raise.
True, but Hitchcock always nails kid roles. Even when they're just existing, they add layers like Hank's toy drum being used to smuggle microfilm. Subtle world building.
Okay, final take. This might be Hitchcock's most human thriller. The stakes are global, but the heart's all family. Also, Jo's refusal to back down, even when the cops doubt her. Iconic.
Alright, who else just finished An Inspector Calls and needs to unpack that ending? My mind is spinning.
Oh totally, David Thewlis as Inspector Ghoul. Chilling the way he just looms in the Burley mansion. You can feel the tension in every scene.
Right, and that whole we're all responsible angle. Classic J B Priestley, but Aisling Walsh's direction made it feel fresh. The close ups on their guilty faces, genius.
Speaking of guilty faces, Ken Stott as Arthur Burling, the capitalist patriarch, his smirk when he denies firing Eva Smith, I wanted to throttle him.

But Miranda Richardson as Misses Burling though, her icy delivery when she blames the girl for being impertinent, pure aristocratic cruelty. Sophie Rundle broke my heart as Eva, that scene where she's fired from the shop.
Ugh, yes. Sheila's meltdown after realizing she got Eva fired over a jealous whim. Chloe Perry nailed that transition from spoiled brat to shattered human.
The timeline twist still gets me. Inspector Ghoul shows up in nineteen twelve, but Eva's death happens after the family secrets are exposed. Is he a ghost, a moral conscience?
And the way everyone backslides once they think he's fake. Eric's drunken confession meant nothing to them. Ken Stodd's final toast to business as usual made me scream.
Aisling Walsh really emphasized the class divide. The Burlings' mansion versus Eva's grimy boarding house. Even the lighting, warm gold for the rich, cold blue for the poor.
That final phone call about a real inspector coming chills. It's not just about one family, it's about every society that ignores its avowals.
Priestley's socialist message hits harder today, David Thewlis said in an interview, that he played Goole as truth itself, unstoppable, inevitable.
Did you catch the name switches? Eva Smith becomes Daisy Renton depending on who's exploiting her. Gerald's affair was the grossest respectable cover up.
Still can't get over Sheila being the only one who grows her line. We're not alone, we're people. Mark drop.
Okay, who else just rewatched Tinker Bell and the Secret of the Wings? I swear this movie gets better every time.
Me, Robert Zemeckis directed this one, right? The animation in the Winter Woods scenes, like the ice crystals and auroras, stunning.
Absolutely, and Mae Whitman as Tinkerbell's voice. She's been voicing her since, what, the eighties? Still perfect.
Don't forget Lucy Hale as the Lily of the Valley fairy. Her character's whole vibe so mysterious but kind. That twist about her knowing Tinker Bell's secret mind blowing.
Right when Tink's wings start glowing and she's freaking out in the library, I love how they tied it to her being a frost talent fairy, like her whole identity crisis is so relatable.
And Timothy Dalton as Lord Milori, his voice is pure gravitas. That moment he reveals the ancient rule about warm and cold fairies, chills literally.
But the real tearjerker is when Tink risks losing her wings to save the Winter Woods. Mae Whitman's delivery when she says, my wings don't make me who I am, waterworks every time.
True. Also, the lore expansion here is genius. Sprite mythology, the four seasons balance, way deeper than just fairy dust and fixing things.
Totally, and the directors nailed the sisterhood theme. Tink and Periwinkle's reunion, I mean, finding out they're twins separated at birth, heartwarming and heartbreaking.
Shoutout to Jeff Bennett as Clank though. His comic relief. I am not built for snow. Classic. Dot. All.
Oh for sure, but let's talk about the music. That orchestral theme when Tink flies over the frozen lake, magical, makes me wanna sprout wings and glide.
Honestly, this might be the best Tinkerbell sequel. The way it tackles belonging and sacrifice way heavier than you'd expect from a kids movie.
Agreed, and that post credits scene with the thawing flowers, perfect setup for more frost adventures. Think they'll ever explore Periwinkle's story next?
Hope so. But even if not, the ending's perfect. Tink embracing both her talents, iconic growth.
Alright, who else just rewatched The River Wild last night? I forgot how intense that rafting scene at Iron Gallet was.

Oh man, Meryl Streep as Gail is a total knockout. Did you know she actually trained for months to handle those rapids? Her screaming, you don't know this river like I do at Kevin Bacon's Wade, chills.

Totally, David Strathairn as Tom broke my heart. Though you can feel the tension between him and Gail from the start, like when they're arguing about the trip while packing gear, so raw.
Curtis Hanson really knew how to balance family drama with thriller stuff. The way he shoots the river, it's like a character itself. Those overhead shots of the rapids, pure anxiety fuel.
And John C Reilly as Terry, he's hilarious but terrifying. That scene where he panics and starts waving the gun around, classic Reilly chaos. But can we talk about the dog? M V P of the movie.
Y E S, when the dog drags Tom out of the water after he escapes, I cheered. But Gale's final showdown with Wade Streep's face when she's steering through Iron Gauntlet and outsmarting him, iconic.

Just rewatched David Lean's Great Expectations last night. Man, that black and white cinematography, stunning. How'd they make marshes look so haunting?
Oh, the Oscar for Best Cinematography was no joke. That shot where young Pip runs through the fog to bring food to Abel Magwitch, chills. Anthony Wager as little Pip nailed the fear and curiosity.

Right, and then adult Pip played by John Mills, such a transformation. The way he carries guilt about abandoning Joe, the blacksmith, heartbreaking. But Valerie Hobson as grown Estella, ice cold, perfect for Miss Havisham's twisted puppet. Chilling.

Miss Havisham's whole vibe, the wedding dress rotting, clocks stopped, pure gothic horror. David Lean really leaned into that decay as metaphor thing. What do you think about the whole benefactor twist? That was pretty wild.

When Magwitch crashes back into Pip's life, mind blown, all that upper class London polish funded by a convict. Social commentary gold. Jean Simmons as young Estella was low key terrifying too, already mastering that break men's hearts act.

Yeah, but Pip's obsession with Estella never sat right with me. Like, dude, she's literally trained to destroy you. But that final scene in the ruined mansion, symbolism overload. Estella's finally free, but Pip's just empty.
Classic Dickens adaptation. Lean kept the bittersweetness. Though I wish they'd shown more of Pip and Joe's reconciliation. That I am your brother line gets me every time.
True. Also, can we talk about how Abel Magwitch's accent shifted? Starts rough, then almost paternal when he reveals he's Pip's sponsor. John Mills' voiceover during Pip's London days, chef's kiss.

Honestly, the whole Great Expectations irony Pip gets riches but loses himself makes you think about class and gratitude. Also, shoutout to whoever designed Miss Havisham's mansion. Cobwebs deserve a supporting actor credit.
Hundred percent that set design Oscar well earned. Lean's camera lingers on every dusty detail, makes you smell the mildew.
Dude, I just rewatched Home Alone for like the twentieth time. Macaulay Culkin as Kevin, still genius. That kid carried the whole movie.
Right, Howie's only eight years old there, the way he screams into the mirror iconic. And Joe Pesci as Harry, that guy's face when he steps on the nail, brutal.
Don't even get me started on Daniel Stern's Marv. His high pitched yelps kill me every time. That paint can to the face moment, pure slapstick gold.
Chris Columbus nailed it, the way he balances chaos with heart. Like when Kevin talks to Old Man Marley later, gets me every time.
Oh man, the traps, the micromachines on the stairs, the blowtorch to the head. Wait, how'd an eight year old even know that stuff?
Suspension of disbelief, Jake. It's all about the fantasy. Plus, John Hurt as the dad totally sells that parental panic. We forgot Kevin. Classic.
True, but my favorite part's the music. That Jingle Bells soundtrack during the burglars montage. Chef's kiss.
Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern deserved Oscars for physical comedy. Did you know Pesci actually burned his hand filming the blowtorch scene?
No way, that's dedication. Also, can we talk about the sequel setup? The family leaves him again in Lost in New York. Parenting fail forever.
The original's untouchable though. Nineties nostalgia. Man, fun fact, it was the highest grossing comedy ever for like two decades.
Makes sense. It's got everything. Heart, laughs, Joe Pesci getting owned by a child. Timeless.

Okay, who else just rewatched All About Eve? I swear, Bette Davis as Margo Channing is still the most iconic performance ever. That voice, fasten your seatbelts, it's going to be a bumpy night. Chills.

Ugh, yes, but let's not forget Ann Baxter as Eve Harrington. The way she switches from timid fan to master manipulator, so subtle it's scary. That scene where she cries to Margo about her tragic past, pure acting gymnastics.
Right, and Celeste Holm as Karen Richards, Margo's too trusting best friend. She's the heart of the movie. But I am always furious when she falls for Eve's act. Like, Karen, open your eyes.
Joseph L. Mankiewicz's script is just chef's kiss. All those snappy one liners and layered power plays. Did you know he wrote it in like six weeks? Insane, right?

The man's a genius. The way he frames Eve lingering in doorways, always half in shadow, you know she's scheming. And George Sanders as Addison DeWitt, that smug, velvet voiced narration, you are maudlin and full of self pity, you are magnificent. Iconic.

Addison's the only one who sees through Eve, but he's just using her for his column. Hollywood eats its own, man. Speaking of Eve's whole I'll do anything to be a star vibe, still relevant with influencer culture today.
Totally, Margo's fear of aging out of the spotlight. Brutal. Bette Davis was only forty two when she played her, but the way she leans into Margo's insecurities, no vanity. Legend.
And the ending, Eve wins the Sarah Siddons Award. But then Phoebe, her own mini Eve, shows up. The cycle never ends. Chilling.
My favorite detail. Bertie Kuhn, Margo's maid, clocking Eve from day one. What a story. Everything but the bloodhounds snapping at her rear end. Thelma Ritter steals every scene she's in.
Birdie's the real M V P. But back to Ann Baxter, how did she not win the Oscar? Oh wait, Bette Davis and she split the vote. Still salty about that.
Classic Hollywood politics, but honestly, the whole cast is fire. Even the minor roles feel lived in. Mankiewicz made a masterpiece about ambition, betrayal, and the cost of fame. Timeless.
Makes you wonder how many real life E's are out there right now scheming their way to the top.
Alright, who else thinks My Fellow Americans is the most underrated political comedy of the nineties? Jack Lemmon and James Garner as ex presidents, genius.
Oh my god, yes, the scene where they're arguing in the diner about tax policy while wearing matching trucker hats. I died laughing.

Right, but it's not just slapstick. Peter Segal actually makes you care about these guys. Former President Matt Douglas and President Russert Crodin hating each other's guts but needing to team up. Perfect odd couple energy.
Dan Aykroyd as the slimy President Cole framing them was chef's kiss. That press conference where he fake cries, spot on satire.
The road trip stuff felt real though, like when they're stuck at that motel arguing about healthcare. Suddenly you remember, they're politicians who've never actually lived normal lives.
And then B A M, armed militants show up. The action scenes were shockingly good. That bridge explosion had me yelling, run Matt, like it was a thriller.
Shoutout to Peter Segal for balancing buddy comedy with actual stakes. The bit where Russell admits he regrets cutting education funding, Jack Lemmon's face, no words, just masterclass acting.
James Garner's delivery of, we're not heroes, we're retirees with a vendetta might be my favorite line. Also their character growth, humbling.
Think the message holds up today. Two ex-presidents realizing they've been out of touch.
Totally, that montage of them working minimum wage jobs, low key profound. Makes you wonder how many politicians actually get it, you know?
True, but let's not overlook the physical comedy. Jack Lemmon trying to climb a fence with those old man grunts. I rewound that three times.
Honestly, the whole bipartisan teamwork angle aged way better than I expected. Also, side note, how has Peter Segal not directed more Oscar bait? Dude's versatile.
We'll talk. Best scene, the finale where they crash the inauguration. Matt quoting Lincoln while Russell distracts the guards with a bad Eames impression. Peak chaos.
With the cherry on top, Cole getting arrested mid-speech, Dan Aykroyd's meltdown, pure camp, love it.

And two legends ribbing each other for two hours, what's not to love?
Alright, who else just finished The Big Knife? I need to unpack that ending.

Right, the way he spirals. Hollywood star by day, existential mess by night. That scene where he smashes his Oscar replica? Chilling.
And Ida Lupino as Marion, his wife. Her quiet desperation killed me. When she says, you are drowning us both, I felt that.
But let's talk about Rod Steiger as Stanley Hoff, the sleazy producer. You are either family or fertilizer. What a line.
Classic Aldrich. No heroes, just broken people. The whole film's a metaphor for selling your soul, right? Charlie's faith crisis isn't just religious, it's about integrity.
Totally, that monologue where Charlie admits he's been playing a hero on screen but a coward in life. Jack Palance deserved an Oscar nomination for that.
But the suicide ending heavy. Do you think he actually saved Marion, or was it just another delusion?
I think it's both. He protects her from Hoff's schemes, but can't escape his own guilt. The gunshot fading into that eerie silence, masterclass in sound design.
And Wendell Corey as the smarmy agent. You are not a has-been, Charlie. You are a never-was, Brutle.
Hollywood blacklist parallels too. Aldrich wasn't subtle. Charlie's fall from grace feels like a dig at the whole studio system.
Yeah, but that's why it works. It's not just a character study, it's a middle finger to fame. Still, that final shot of Marion alone in the spotlight, devastating.
Agreed. Not a feel good flick, but man, it sticks with you. Aldrich and Palin's unmatched combo.
Anyone else obsessed with the Murder at the Vicarage? Geraldine McEwan as Miss Marple is perfection.
Oh totally, her little observations while knitting so sly. Charlie Palmer really gets Christie's vibe, cozy but vicious.
Ugh, Colonel Protheroe deserved what he got. Who threatens a vicar in his own study? But wait, did anyone not want him dead?

Geraldine's delivery there, iconic. But let's talk about the actual murder setup. Prothero's body in the vicar's study. Genius. Irony. Perfection.
Charlie Palmer framed St Mary Mead perfectly. All those gossipy villagers, Miss Marple's eyes missing nothing. That overhead shot of the village square, it just...
Did you catch the clock alibi trick? Palmer nailed Christie's misdirection. I rewound twice to spot the time discrepancy.
But McEwan's quiet moments killed me, like when she tells the vicar, guilt wears many faces. Chills, literal chills.
Vicar Clements breakdown though. I wished him dead, but not like this. Talk about tragic irony. That stained glass window lighting, chef's kiss.
Rachel Sterling's reaction shots were everything. Mrs. Clements' hands trembling while pouring tea, no dialogue needed. Chilling.
Still think the gardener's shovel was a red herring? Miss Marple totally knew the real weapon from the start. Classic human nature monologue.
Charlie Palmer better direct all the Marple adaptations. This one's way sharper than those glossy Poirot remakes.
True, but the ending felt rushed. The book had three confessions. Palmer streamlined it, but I missed that chaos.
Nah, the single culprit work that final shot of Miss Marple knitting as village peace returns bone chilling. Murder never sleeps.
Can we talk about Jenny McTeer as the nosy maid? Her harmless gossip actually mattered. Palmer hid clues in plain sight.
Geraldine McEwan deserves another B A F T A, the way she inhales before dropping truth bombs. Legendary.
Next up, A Pocket Full of Rye, Mc Ewan's Marple meets her own cinematic universe.
Alright, who's seen Moneyball recently? I just rewatched it and man, Brad Pitt as Billy Beane is next level.
Oh totally, that scene where he trades his star players, gut wrenching. But Jonah Hill as Peter Brand, who knew he could pull off a nerdy stats guy so well.
Right, Philip Seymour Hoffman as Art Howe, the old school manager, was such a perfect foil. The tension between him and Billy Shears, Kiss, was just.
And Robin Wright as Sharon, Billy's ex-wife. She's barely in it, but that diner scene where she tells him to stop running from failure, chills.
Don't forget the whole sabermetrics angle, using math to beat rich teams like the Yankees. Genius. But do you think it oversimplifies the real story?
Maybe, but Bennett Miller's direction keeps it grounded. The close-ups during the trade calls, you feel Billy's desperation.
True, and the soundtrack, those minimalist piano notes when Billy's driving alone, so haunting. It's not just a baseball movie, it's about obsession.
Speaking of that montage where they recruit undervalued players, Scott Hattaway swinging a trash can lid, hilarious and weirdly inspiring.
The real kicker is the ending. Oakland wins twenty games in a row, but still loses the playoffs. Why, it's not a Hollywood script.
Exactly, the film's based on Michael Lewis's book, right? It's really about challenging tradition, adapt or die.
Brad Pitt's "How can you not get romantic about baseball?" line kills me every time. It's like he's defending his own madness.
Madness or not, the A's changed the game. Now every team uses on base percentage stats. Billy's legacy is real.
Still, imagine being Art Howe. Dude just wanted to bunt and steal bases. Can't blame him for resisting Billy's bellmouled revolution.
Robin White's Sharon probably saved Billy's soul. Though without her pushing him to face his fears, he'd still be smashing radios.
Anyone else think the movie Lowkey roasted the Yankees? T here is rich teams, poor teams, then fifty feet of crap savage.
Yeah, just rewatched Where the Wild Things Are for the millionth time. Spike Jonze really nailed that bittersweet childhood vibe, huh?
Oh man, Max Records as that wild kid Max, perfect casting. The way he throws tantrums feels so real, like when he bites his mom, Katherine Keener's face in that scene, brutal.
For real, and James Gandolfini voicing Carol, the saddest monster ever, his angry outbursts masking loneliness, chills. Spike Jonze made those puppets breathe, man. No C G I fluff.
Right, the practical effects are insane. Those giant fursuits and the way they stomp around felt like a kid's imagination come alive. But that island, it's not all fun, is it?
Nah, it's dark. Max thinks being king'll fix everything, but the monsters' fights mirror his own family chaos. Like Carol smashing huts because Max can't keep everyone happy. Hits hard.
And don't forget Lauren Ambrose as K W, her gentle voice balancing Carol's rage. That scene where she hides Max in her stomach, so weirdly comforting yet creepy.
Spot on, said. The book's only ten sentences. He stretched it into a whole emotional journey. The ending where Max sails back, no big speeches, just him hugging his mom. Waterworks every time.
Kathryn Hahn is so underrated as the mom. She's exhausted but loving, like when she chases Max outside yelling, come back, but lets him run. Parenting in a nutshell.
Still can't believe they built that entire forest set. The wild rumpus dance with torches, pure madness. But Carol's final roar as Max leaves, man, that's grief.
